note: Detriment, not benefit: giving up a lawful freedom at the promisor's request is consideration whether or not the promisor gains anything.
An exclusive agent's implied promise of reasonable efforts keeps the deal from being illusory and supplies consideration (New York).

In this English domestic arrangement the wife did not establish the alleged contractual exchange; Atkin separately emphasized the absence of intent to create legal obligations. The judges’ rationales should not be collapsed.
Giving up a claim that proves invalid is consideration if it was asserted with an honest and reasonable belief in its validity (Maryland).
A purchase conditioned on the buyer's satisfaction is not illusory, because he must judge satisfaction honestly and in good faith (California).
Second Restatement: consideration is a bargained-for exchange (§ 71), and a surrendered claim counts if doubtful or honestly believed (§ 74).
Iowa adopts § 74: a claim later shown invalid still supports a settlement if it was doubtful or the claimant honestly believed it might be valid.
A requirements contract has consideration even before the buyer has any requirements: § 2-306 binds it to buy its good-faith needs (Missouri law).
Cardozo reads a duty of reasonable efforts into an exclusive agency: courts supply the obligation the business arrangement implies.

For goods, § 2-306(2) imposes best efforts in exclusive dealing unless otherwise agreed; subsection (1) separately measures output or requirements by good faith and limits disproportionate quantities.
Best efforts does not demand ruinous losses, but a brewer may not neglect the brand it promised to promote to raise its overall profit (New York law).
The Second Restatement states a duty of good faith in performance and enforcement. It is persuasive common-law authority; a jurisdiction must adopt or apply the proposition.
Posner: good faith forbids deliberately exploiting the other side's oversight about its contract rights, though it does not require altruism.
A party must actually exercise a discretion it promised to exercise, and not arbitrarily, but good faith adds no duty the contract excludes (New York).
Singapore declines to imply a general duty of good faith in law; a term is implied in fact only where necessary.

The Airline Deregulation Act preempts this state-imposed covenant claim because it relates to airline prices, routes or services and enlarges voluntarily assumed obligations; ordinary contractual promises remain a separate question.
A promise of a home to a relative is a gratuity: her costly move in reliance on it does not make it enforceable (Alabama).
Equitable estoppel bars the no-consideration defense when the promisor induced the promisee to give up her job in reliance on his note (Nebraska).
First Restatement § 90: a promise one should expect to induce definite and substantial action, which does, binds if only enforcement avoids injustice.
Traynor carries § 90 into commerce: a subcontractor's bid becomes irrevocable once the general contractor relies on it in bidding (California).
A pension promise binds under § 90 because the employee retired in reliance on it, though her past service was no consideration (Missouri).
Wisconsin applies § 90 to failed franchise negotiations: reliance losses are recoverable though the promises were too indefinite for a contract.

The Second Restatement omits “definite and substantial,” permits a remedy limited as justice requires, and excuses proof of induced reliance for charitable subscriptions and marriage settlements. Adoption varies by jurisdiction.
Reliance on an at-will assurance earns reliance damages, such as a lost sale price, not the profits the relationship would have brought (Indiana law).
After the Supreme Court held the First Amendment no bar, Minnesota enforces a reporter's promise of source confidentiality by promissory estoppel.
Texas: promissory estoppel avoids the statute of frauds for loan agreements only if the lender promised to sign a writing that satisfies it.

A separate criminal-law branch: Pennsylvania enforces a prosecutor’s unconditional nonprosecution assurance after detrimental reliance affecting self-incrimination. This is due process, not an ordinary § 90 contract holding.
A promise to hold an offer open, given without consideration, does not bind; the offeror may revoke, and word from a third party is enough notice.

For an offer inviting performance rather than a return promise, beginning or tendering the invited performance protects an opportunity to complete it. The offeror’s duty remains conditional on completion; preparation alone is a separate question.
Learned Hand: a supplier's bid used in a contractor's bid stays revocable, and promissory estoppel does not hold an offer that sought a bargain.
New York: a signed written offer that states it is irrevocable binds for the stated period, or a reasonable time, without consideration.

A merchant’s signed assurance to hold a goods offer open needs no consideration for the stated or reasonable time, capped at three months under § 2-205. An assurance on the offeree’s form must be separately signed.
Reliance makes an offer irrevocable: a subcontractor's bid binds for a reasonable time once the general contractor used it in a winning bid.

The Second Restatement follows Drennan’s reliance rationale: foreseeable substantial reliance before acceptance can bind an offer as an option to the extent necessary to avoid injustice, not automatically for every use of a bid.
Acceptance needs an outward act put in the course of communication to the offeror; private preparations to perform are not enough (New York).

Objective legal commitment depends on context. This English domestic support arrangement did not establish the contract alleged; ordinary family arrangements are not automatically enforceable bargains.
The offeror controls the manner: an order that makes home-office approval the acceptance needs no separate notice of that approval (Texas).
Unless the offer clearly says otherwise, acceptance may be made in any reasonable manner, including a prompt promise to ship or prompt shipment.
Assent is read from outward words and acts as a reasonable person would take them; a secret intent to joke does not undo a signed sale (Virginia).
An advertisement that is clear, definite and leaves nothing open is an offer; the store cannot add a 'women only' rule after acceptance (Minnesota).
An acceptance must be an unequivocal commitment; a reply showing readiness while asking for more information is not one (North Dakota).
The mirror-image rule: a reply that varies the offer's terms is a counteroffer that rejects the offer, which cannot later be revived.
For sales of goods the Code drops the mirror-image rule: an acceptance can form a contract though it adds or changes terms.
An acceptance is expressly conditional only if it clearly says the offeree will not proceed without assent to its terms; 'subject to' is not enough.
When forms do not form a contract but both sides perform, § 2-207(3) supplies the terms the writings share plus Code gap-fillers.
Different terms in offer and acceptance knock each other out and Code gap-fillers replace them: the majority rule, predicted for Illinois.

Between merchants an additional term enters unless § 2-207(2) excludes it: the offer limits acceptance, the addition materially alters the deal, or timely objection occurs. Bayway assigns the material-alteration burden to the party opposing inclusion.
A liability limit printed on a claim check binds only with reasonable notice and assent; taking the ticket is not assent as a matter of law (New York).
A non-negotiated forum clause in a form ticket is enforceable if reasonable and fundamentally fair; notice of the clause was conceded.
Terms in the box: following ProCD, a seller may invite acceptance by keeping the goods, so enclosed terms bind a buyer who does not return them.
The buyer ordinarily is the offeror, so terms shipped in the box are proposals under § 2-207 that bind a consumer only on express assent.
Online terms bind only if the screen reasonably shows they exist and that clicking means assent; terms hidden below a download button did not.

The Federal Arbitration Act preempts California’s Discover Bank rule when it conditions arbitration enforcement on classwide procedures. This federal preemption holding does not validate every standard term or eliminate generally applicable contract defenses.
Inquiry notice suffices: a clear sign-up screen linking the terms binds a user who registers, without an 'I agree' box (California law).

On this record, website posting and continued use did not give sufficient notice of an arbitration amendment. A separate retroactivity analysis excludes the remaining pre-amendment claims; post-amendment claims had been dismissed by stipulation.
Leaving the price and how long it would run for later agreement makes an unenforceable agreement to agree; the court will not supply them (New York).
A sale of goods does not fail for open terms if the parties meant to contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for a remedy.
Reliance in negotiations: Wisconsin awards reliance losses on promises made during franchise talks that were too indefinite for a contract.
A letter of intent with an express promise to negotiate in good faith can itself be an enforceable contract (Pennsylvania law predicted).
When parties meant to stay bound and their pricing mechanism fails, a court may set a reasonable price and supervise continued performance (Ohio).
New York promissory estoppel yields reliance damages, including attributable overhead, when talks never produced the contemplated contract.
A lender's promise to consider a loan modification, inducing the borrower to default, can support promissory estoppel (Massachusetts law predicted).
France codifies good faith in negotiations: fault in negotiating yields damages, but never the benefits expected from the unmade contract.
A promise of extra pay for work the promisees were already bound to do lacks consideration and does not bind.
New York: a signed written agreement to modify or discharge a contract does not fail for lack of consideration.
Parties may rescind and replace a deal in one transaction; an owner who freely gives up the old price after unforeseen rock is bound (New Hampshire).
An agreement modifying a sales contract needs no consideration; the Code's comments police modifications by a test of good faith instead.

A separate validity limit: even a modification with consideration is voidable for economic duress when threatened withholding leaves no timely substitute or adequate breach remedy. This does not loosen the pre-existing-duty rule.
The Code lets a court refuse to enforce a contract or clause it finds unconscionable when made, without defining the term.
Courts may refuse to enforce a contract unconscionable when made: absence of meaningful choice plus terms unreasonably favorable to the other side.
California: adhesion terms bind unless outside reasonable expectations or unduly oppressive; one side's own ally cannot be sole arbitrator.
California applies a sliding scale of procedural and substantive unconscionability and refuses a one-sided mandatory employment arbitration agreement.
Oklahoma applies the two-part test: a hidden, one-sided litter clause the buyers could not understand is unconscionable as a matter of law.
The FAA preempts a state rule, framed as unconscionability, that conditions arbitration agreements on the availability of class procedures.
After Concepcion, unconscionability remains a general defense to arbitration, and several one-sided terms can defeat the whole agreement (California).
Where the writing is complete on a subject, an oral term the parties would naturally have put in it is barred, even as a separate deal (Pennsylvania).
New York: a prior oral term is provable only if collateral in form, consistent with the writing, and not one the parties would ordinarily put in it.

Ambiguous “chicken” is read through negotiations, trade evidence and regulatory usage; the buyer failed to prove the narrower meaning. This is interpretation of the agreed description, not a freestanding parol-evidence exception.
The rule does not bar reformation: a term left out by mutual mistake may be proved and written back in (Pennsylvania).
California admits a collateral oral term the parties might naturally have made separately, unless the writing was meant as the whole bargain.
Extrinsic evidence is admissible whenever relevant to a meaning the words are reasonably susceptible to, however plain the writing looks (California).
Trade usage and course of performance can supplement the written price term when reasonably consistent with it. The Hawaii asphalt-market evidence supported price protection in this transaction.
Under Pacific Gas even an unambiguous clause must be opened to extrinsic evidence; the Ninth Circuit applies the rule while criticizing it.
New York's answer: extrinsic evidence may not be used to create an ambiguity in a complete, clear and unambiguous writing.
New York again reads the writing on its face: silence about a use does not make a clear, unconditional transfer of ownership ambiguous.
Under the CISG, which has no parol evidence rule, a merger clause binds only if both parties meant it to; negotiations count under Article 8.
Trade usage may give seemingly plain words or figures a special trade meaning, with no prior finding of ambiguity (Oregon).

The 1952 Code’s §§ 1-205 and 2-202 admit dealing and trade usage to explain or supplement a writing. Revised Article 1 combines context rules in § 1-303: express terms generally prevail, but course of performance can show waiver or modification under §§ 1-303(f) and 2-209.
The party claiming the narrower meaning of an ambiguous term must prove it, and a usage binds a newcomer only if known or so general as to be presumed.
Under the Code, usage and dealing come in without ambiguity unless irreconcilable with the express terms; a merger clause must expressly negate them.
Trade usage and course of performance can qualify an express posted-price term with price protection if reasonably consistent with it.
Usage can cut the other way: an unrebutted trade usage supplied an exclusive repair-or-refund remedy as part of the agreement.
A buyer need not disclose market news equally open to both sides, but neither party may say or do anything to mislead the other.
Caveat emptor: a seller's silence about a known hidden defect is not actionable without a false statement, half-truth or duty to speak (Massachusetts).
Opinions can be actionable misrepresentations when the speaker has superior knowledge or the parties are unequal in judging the subject (Florida).
Half-truths: one who speaks on a subject must disclose what is needed to keep the statement from misleading; Swinton is distinguished (Massachusetts).
Florida abandons caveat emptor for home sales: a seller must disclose known facts, not readily observable, that materially affect value.
Aspirational sales talk is puffery, not fraud, and Illinois promissory fraud needs a scheme to defraud beyond one broken promise.
New York: a specific disclaimer of reliance on statements about the very matter at issue bars a claim of fraudulent inducement.
Mansfield: the order of performance follows the parties' evident sense; giving security was a condition precedent to the sale of the business.
An express condition of personal satisfaction is enforced: a buyer who reserved the right to reject a portrait he disliked need not pay (Michigan).
Divisibility limits forfeiture: where the price is set per unit, the performer recovers for each unit fully delivered (Pennsylvania).
Waiver: an owner who kept paying without asking for the architect's certificates cannot invoke their absence against final payment (Pennsylvania).

Substantial performance limits forfeiture for an innocent, trivial construction deviation where the requirement is treated as a promise or constructive condition. It does not generally replace strict compliance with an unmistakable express condition.
An express condition must occur as stated: a mortgage commitment above the agreed rate fails it, whatever substitute the seller offers (Connecticut).
An ambiguous pay-when-paid clause fixes a time for payment, not a condition; shifting the owner's credit risk needs clear words (Florida).
Where performance depends on a particular thing, its destruction without fault excuses both sides: the law implies a condition.
A builder's absolute promise binds despite unforeseen soil; hardship short of impossibility is no excuse (Minnesota).
Mistake at formation: a sale may be avoided when both parties erred about the substance of the thing, not merely its quality (Michigan).
Frustration of purpose: when the shared foundation of the deal fails, the parties are discharged though performance is still possible.
California accepts frustration but confines it: the event must be unforeseeable and destroy nearly all the value of the return performance.
Impracticability needs an unexpected event, a risk not allocated by agreement or custom, and real impracticability; extra cost alone did not suffice.
Arizona rescinds for a mutual mistake about a basic assumption (Restatement (Second) § 152) but limits the buyer to restitution, not reliance costs.
When replacing innocent defective work would cost far more than the value it adds, the measure is diminution in value (New York).
Minnesota awards the cost of the promised grading for a deliberate breach, though it far exceeds the value the work would add to the land.
Repair cost for defects reasonably fixable; diminution in value where the fix would mean tearing out work, as with the misplaced wall (Wisconsin).
Oklahoma caps damages at diminution in value when the broken term was incidental and its cost grossly exceeds the value it would add.
England's middle course: rebuilding cost is out when unreasonable, but the owner may recover for loss of amenity rather than nothing.
Recoverable losses arise naturally from breach or were within both parties' contemplation when contracting; uncommunicated special losses are out.
Avoidable loss: after a clear repudiation the other party may not keep performing and charge the cost; recovery is costs to date plus profit.
Mitigation: an employee's damages are reduced only by earnings from comparable work; a different or inferior job may be refused (California).
Certainty: a new business is not barred from lost profits; a reasonable basis for estimating them suffices, though the jury may not guess (Michigan).
New York: twenty years of projected stadium profits are too speculative, and the county never contemplated liability for them.
New York requires that liability for an unusual loss was contemplated at contracting, stricter than mere foreseeability, and denies land appreciation.
Expectation: the value of the promised result minus the value of what was delivered; pain the operation would have caused anyway is not compensated.
Restitution for the party in breach: a builder short of substantial performance recovers the benefit conferred less the owner's damages (Idaho).
Contract damages compensate: punitive damages are unavailable even for a malicious breach unless a tort is pleaded and proved (Wisconsin).

On a doctor's promise of a result, the patient recovers expenses, worsening, and pain and distress beyond what the treatment entailed, items the court found recoverable on either a reliance or an expectation measure.
Restitution for the injured party: a subcontractor who quits after a material breach recovers the value conferred, not reduced by its losing bargain.
Ordinary contract damages measure the plaintiff's loss; the breacher's gains count only insofar as they track that loss.
Colorado allows disgorgement for a conscious, substantial breach where damages are inadequate, less profits due to the breacher's own contribution.
Equity will not compel a singer to perform, but it will enjoin her breach of an express promise not to sing elsewhere during the engagement.

A buyer of goods may obtain specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances. Inability to obtain substitutes can support relief beyond a uniqueness label; damages’ adequacy and equitable discretion still matter.
A horse trained by the buyer has unique value to him, so equity orders its delivery despite the usual rule for chattels (Arkansas).
On this record the used jet was not shown to be unique, and a higher replacement price does not make damages inadequate, so specific performance under § 2-716 fails.
Posner: an injunction against breach of an exclusivity covenant is proper when damages are inadequate, judged by the costs and benefits of each remedy.
A fixed sum is liquidated damages, not a penalty, if harm was hard to estimate at formation and the sum was a reasonable forecast (South Dakota).
A formula paying full revenue without deducting the costs the promisee saves is a penalty; Posner questions the rule but applies it (Illinois law).
New Jersey tests reasonableness in all the circumstances and presumes a clause between commercial equals valid; the challenger bears the burden.
The assigned translated Swiss decision permits judicial reduction of excessive contractual penalties. This comparative account does not establish the rule in an American jurisdiction.
New York lets a creditor of the promisee sue the promisor on a promise made for his benefit, though he was no party and gave no consideration.
Donee beneficiaries: a niece may enforce a promise made to her dying aunt for her benefit; closeness of kinship is not a strict limit (New York).
A city's water-supply contract benefits the public only incidentally; a resident may sue only if it promised compensation to individuals (New York).

The Second Restatement replaces its creditor/donee terminology with intended and incidental beneficiaries, conditioned on the contracting parties’ intention. It proposes a framework; it does not enact a uniform state rule.
South Dakota presumes against private enforcement of government contracts; an inmate is incidental to the State's food-service contract.
The same day: a settlement that expressly covers every Jewish inmate who asks for kosher meals is enforceable by a member of that class.
Power runs with territory: a personal judgment needs in-state service or a voluntary appearance, so an absent nonresident is out of reach.
Minimum contacts replace physical presence: suit is allowed if it does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.
A single contract with a substantial connection to the forum supports a suit on that contract.
Purposeful availment: the defendant must itself reach into the forum; the unilateral acts of others do not count.
Stream of commerce in a state court: a component maker can be sued where its product, sold through ordinary distribution, causes injury.
Acquiescing in a child's move to the forum is not purposeful availment, so the parent cannot be sued there for support.
Foreseeable travel of a product is not enough; the defendant's own conduct must make suit there foreseeable, as when it serves that market.

Regular, substantial circulation in the forum supported jurisdiction over the libel claim despite the plaintiff’s limited forum ties; the jurisdictional inquiry concerns the defendant’s forum conduct.
The intentional tort was expressly aimed at California, where the story and injury were centered. The effects analysis depends on defendant-created forum connections.
Two steps, contacts then fairness: a long-term franchise deal aimed at a forum company is a contact even without physical entry.
Eight Justices agree the remaining foreign indemnity suit is unreasonable. No majority chooses between awareness and additional forum-directed conduct as the stream-of-commerce contact test.

Six Justices reject jurisdiction, with no five-Justice rationale: four require state targeting; two concur on the isolated-sale record and decline a broader rule. The three dissenters take a broader market approach.
The defendant’s own contacts must connect him to the forum itself; knowledge of the plaintiffs’ forum connections and foreseeable injury there did not supply those contacts.
Relatedness is claim by claim: nonresidents' claims need their own link to the forum, and the sliding-scale approach is rejected.
'Arise out of or relate to' needs no strict causation: a maker that cultivates a market for a model can be sued where it injures.

A separate federal-statute branch: the Fifth Amendment does not import the Fourteenth Amendment’s minimum-contacts test. This targeted terrorism statute is valid; the Court leaves the outer limits and a separate reasonableness requirement open.
Regular magazine sales in a state support a libel suit there, even for nationwide damages and though the plaintiff has no ties to it.
Effects test: individuals whose alleged intentional tort was aimed at the forum, knowing the harm would be felt there, can be sued there.
A sliding scale for websites: knowing online business with forum residents supports jurisdiction; a passive site does not.
The defendant's own conduct must connect him to the forum itself; an injury the plaintiff feels there is not enough, even for torts.
After Walden, a website's reach and interactivity in a state do not support a libel suit unless the story or site was aimed there.
Continuous and substantial activity in a state may justify suit there even on claims unrelated to that activity.
A foreign company run from an Ohio office during wartime may be sued there on unrelated claims; due process permits it.
Purchases, training trips and a single negotiating visit are not the continuous and systematic contacts needed for unrelated claims.
General jurisdiction only where the corporation is essentially at home; products reaching the state through commerce do not count.
'At home' means place of incorporation and principal place of business, save an exceptional case; heavy in-state business is not enough.
A railroad with extensive in-state track and workers is still not at home there, and FELA's venue clause confers no jurisdiction.

Pennsylvania registration under an express consent statute satisfies the Due Process Clause under Pennsylvania Fire. This is separate from “at home” contacts; the Commerce Clause challenge was left for remand.
Jurisdiction rests on in-state service, voluntary appearance, or local property seized at the outset; consent and status cases are reserved.
A debt follows the debtor: serving him on a brief visit lets the state seize what he owes an absent creditor.
Implied consent: driving on a state's roads appoints a state official to receive service in suits about the driving, with notice to the driver.
Presence obtained by fraud does not count: a defendant lured into the state and served can attack the judgment where it is enforced.
Domicile suffices for a personal judgment against an absent resident given proper notice; 'fair play and substantial justice' starts here.
Trickery by the party's lawyer that brings a nonresident into the state to be served also voids the service.

The appointed process agent’s actual prompt forwarding validates service under the Federal Rule despite no advance promise to forward. The Court reserves failed notice and decides no due-process question; it does not approve every boilerplate forum term.
Property alone no longer suffices: every assertion of jurisdiction, in rem or quasi in rem, must meet the Shoe standard.
Personal jurisdiction is a waivable individual right, so a discovery sanction may establish the facts that support it.
Tag jurisdiction survives Shaffer: personal service on a visitor inside the state is enough, though no rationale won a majority.

Pennsylvania registration under an express consent statute satisfies the Due Process Clause under Pennsylvania Fire. This is separate from “at home” contacts; the Commerce Clause challenge was left for remand.
Notice must be reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to inform interested parties and let them be heard.
Freezing a worker's wages before judgment without notice and a prior hearing violates due process, even though it is temporary.
A hearing comes before the state helps seize household goods, even briefly and with title disputed, save extraordinary situations.

Mitchell sustains Louisiana sequestration for a lien creditor on sworn facts before a judge, with a creditor bond and an immediate debtor hearing. These safeguards qualify Fuentes; not every judge-issued seizure is valid.
Garnishment issued by a clerk on a conclusory affidavit, with no judge and no early hearing, still violates due process.
The process due is set by balancing the private interest, the risk of error and value of safeguards, and the government's interest.
Mathews adapted for private remedies: attaching a home ex parte without exigency fails; the creditor's interest takes the state's place.
Federal courts decide questions of general commercial law for themselves; state decisions are respected but not binding.
Swift at its height: a company reincorporates to create diversity and escape a state rule, and the federal court lets it.
There is no federal general common law: in diversity cases state law, including state court decisions, supplies the rule of decision.
Outcome determination: a state limitations bar applies because ignoring it would change the result of the suit.
A state rule that only service stops the limitations clock governs a diversity suit, though Rule 3 dates commencement from filing.
A state statute closing its courts to an unqualified foreign corporation closes the federal court in that state too.
A state law requiring security for expenses applies in a federal derivative suit; the Federal Rule then in force did not conflict.
Outcome is not everything: a state practice not bound up with the right yields to strong federal interests such as the jury's role.
The outcome test is read through Erie's twin aims, discouraging forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws.
Reaffirms Ragan: Rule 3 governs commencement for federal procedural purposes, while the integral state service rule determines limitations tolling. There is no direct collision.
Accommodation: a state limit on excessive verdicts applies, enforced by the federal trial judge and reviewed for abuse of discretion.
The Rules Enabling Act lets the Supreme Court make procedural rules that do not abridge, enlarge or modify substantive rights.
A Rule is valid if it really regulates procedure; the importance of the interest it touches does not make it substantive.
Rule 3 does not determine when the state limitations period is tolled. The state service requirement applies; Walker later reaffirms this result after Hanna.

Rule 35 can reach a defendant as well as a plaintiff, but requires a genuine controversy about the condition and good cause for the particular examination; procedural examination does not itself change substantive rights.
A valid Federal Rule that covers the issue applies even if the outcome differs; Erie's twin-aims test does not decide Rules cases.
No direct collision: Rule 3 does not govern state tolling, so Ragan stands and state service law applies.
A federal rule broad enough to collide with state law controls: an appellate sanctions rule displaces a mandatory state penalty.
The same test for federal statutes: § 1404(a) covers a forum clause's effect on transfer, so state hostility to the clause yields.
Rule 41(b) does not prescribe the claim-preclusive effect of a diversity judgment. Federal common law ordinarily borrows the forum state’s preclusion law, subject to federal interests.

Five Justices let the Rule 23 class proceed despite New York’s penalty-class bar. No majority adopts one validity test: Scalia’s plurality reads procedure categorically; Stevens asks whether the state rule defines substantive rights.

The majority finds Rule 8, reinforced by Rule 12, incompatible with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement. Jackson agrees with the judgment through Rules 3 and 12 while rejecting the majority’s Rule 8 collision analysis.
No federal general common law: federal courts may not make their own rules for ordinary state-law disputes.
Federal law governs the United States' rights on its own commercial paper, and courts may fashion that law absent a statute.
Federal law decides whether a release of FELA rights is valid even in state court, and a state that uses juries cannot take the fraud issue from one.
Clearfield stops where the United States' rights are not at stake: private disputes over government paper follow state law.
A uniquely federal interest plus a significant conflict displaces state tort law: the defense for military contractors.

Federal common law governs the claim-preclusive effect of a federal diversity judgment and ordinarily incorporates the preclusion law of the state where the federal court sat, unless that law is incompatible with a federal interest; Rule 41(b) does not itself prescribe that effect.
Federal common law only where needed to protect uniquely federal interests; a judge-made rule for dividing tax refunds falls.
The Federal Rules replace the code's 'facts constituting a cause of action' with a short and plain statement showing a right to relief.
An inartful, home-drawn complaint survives because it shows some claim; the old cause-of-action formula no longer governs.

Under the Missouri special-damages rule, the additional injury claims required specific pleading. Actual knowledge outside the pleading did not substitute for amendment; this is a state-law illustration, not a Supreme Court reading of Rule 9(g).
Reads the complaint as a whole when considering publication and privilege, and applies the distinct functions of Rule 12(b)(6), 12(e) and 12(f).
Fair notice is enough: dismiss only if it appears beyond doubt that no set of facts could support relief.
Code pleading holds out: North Carolina still demands the ultimate facts, not labels such as 'assault' and 'trespass'.
A statutory damages limitation operates as an affirmative defense that must be pleaded; the government’s failure to raise it timely forfeited the defense in this litigation.
No heightened pleading outside Rule 9(b): a discrimination complaint need not plead the facts of a prima facie case.
Plausibility replaces 'no set of facts': parallel conduct plus a bare assertion of agreement does not state a conspiracy.
Under the PSLRA's heightened standard, the inference of scienter must be cogent and at least as compelling as any innocent one.
Plausibility governs every civil action: set aside legal conclusions, then ask whether the remaining facts plausibly show liability.
Rule 9(b) reaches any claim that rests on a unified course of fraudulent conduct, even when fraud is not an element.
Plausibility is not probability: a coherent, case-specific story of what happened, who did it and why it is unlawful suffices.

Rule 8(b) requires an admission, denial or genuine lack of knowledge after reasonable inquiry. Calling an allegation a legal conclusion does not excuse an answer; the court ordered amendment rather than automatically entering judgment.
Theory of the pleadings: a complaint framed as conversion fails as conversion and cannot be saved as a claim in contract.
Rule 15 lets parties amend freely, conform pleadings to the evidence tried, and relate amendments back to the original filing.
Leave to amend is freely given; the opponent must show actual prejudice, which is not presumed when an admission is withdrawn.
Trial by consent of an unpleaded issue requires that the opponent knew it was being tried; evidence relevant to pleaded issues is not consent.
Relation back for a new defendant required notice within the limitations period itself, not the added time for service.
Notice to the new defendant within the time allowed for service now suffices, so a misnamed party can be substituted after limitations runs.
Relation back turns on what the new defendant knew or should have known, not on the plaintiff's knowledge or diligence.

A separate starting point in derivative verification: good-faith reliance on an adviser’s investigation sustains the shareholder’s verification. This is not a holding that subjective good faith defeats modern Rule 11 sanctions.
Rule 11 gains teeth: signers owe an objective duty of reasonable inquiry, and courts must sanction violations.
Under the 1983 rule a represented party who signs a paper owes an objective duty of inquiry; relying on counsel is no excuse.
The 1993 rule makes sanctions discretionary, aims them at deterrence, and gives a 21-day safe harbor to withdraw a challenged paper.
A party's sanctions motion must honor the safe harbor, and a lawyer may rely on objectively reasonable information from the client.

The district court applies Rule 11 to invented citations and knowing falsehoods or conscious avoidance after warnings. Its bad-faith requirement addresses court-initiated sanctions in that circuit; the party-motion route has a separate safe harbor.
Article III reaches any case in which a federal question forms an ingredient, the broad constitutional ceiling.
Congress grants general federal-question jurisdiction in words like Article III's, later read far more narrowly.
A suit Congress authorizes is not for that reason one arising under federal law when local rules and custom decide it.
Well-pleaded complaint rule: the federal question must appear in the plaintiff's own claim, not in an anticipated defense.
Holmes's creation test: a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action.
A state-law claim can arise under federal law when it necessarily turns on a substantial federal question.
Artful pleading: a plaintiff cannot defeat removal by dressing a claim that is really federal in state-law words.
A federal standard embedded in a state tort claim is not substantial enough when Congress gave no private federal remedy.
No federal cause of action is required: the federal issue must be necessarily raised, disputed, substantial, and fit the federal-state balance.
Substantial means important to the federal system as a whole; a malpractice claim about a patent case stays in state court.
Pendent jurisdiction begins narrow: a court may decide a second ground for the same cause of action, not a separate state claim.
Common nucleus of operative fact: related state claims may be heard with a substantial federal claim, at the court's discretion.
Compulsory counterclaims, read by logical relationship, fall within ancillary jurisdiction without a basis of their own.
Pendent parties: a court must ask whether Congress negated jurisdiction over them; a county excluded from § 1983 stays out.
A plaintiff cannot use ancillary jurisdiction to sue a nondiverse third-party defendant; complete diversity would be evaded.
No pendent-party jurisdiction without express authorization from Congress, which prompted § 1367.
Congress codifies supplemental jurisdiction over the whole case or controversy, with limits in diversity cases and room to decline.
In diversity, one plaintiff's qualifying claim carries co-plaintiffs and class members below the amount, but not nondiverse parties.
When a plaintiff amends away every federal claim after removal, supplemental jurisdiction ends with it and the case is remanded.
Each holder of a joint interest must be able to sue or be sued in federal court, the root of the complete-diversity rule.
Complete diversity is a reading of the statute: Article III needs only minimal diversity, so Congress may use it, as in interpleader.
Each class member with a separate claim must meet the amount in controversy; one qualifying claim cannot carry the rest.
Citizenship means domicile, which persists until a new home is taken with intent to remain, and is tested when suit is filed.
The amount claimed in good faith controls unless it is legally certain the claim is smaller, and the plaintiff gets a chance to show it.

CAFA permits qualifying classes with minimal diversity, an aggregate amount exceeding $5 million and ordinarily at least 100 members, subject to statutory exclusions and exceptions. Ordinary § 1332(a) complete diversity remains.
Through § 1367 one plaintiff's qualifying claim carries others below the amount, but a single nondiverse plaintiff still defeats jurisdiction.
Complete diversity missing at removal is not cured by wrongly dismissing the nondiverse defendant; the merits judgment is vacated.
Removal statutes are read strictly: a plaintiff who faces a counterclaim is still a plaintiff and cannot remove.
CAFA lets any defendant remove a class action without the others' consent, even a forum citizen, and drops the one-year limit.
A named plaintiff's stipulation cannot hold a class below CAFA's amount, because before certification it does not bind the class.
A notice of removal needs only a plausible allegation of the amount, with evidence only if challenged; no presumption against CAFA removal.
Only the original defendant may remove: a third-party counterclaim defendant cannot, under § 1441(a) or CAFA.
Jurisdiction cannot be conferred by choice: even the plaintiff who picked federal court wins reversal when the record fails to show it.
A state high court holds that a missed statutory element, here divorce residency, does not strip the court of power or void its judgment.
Clear-statement rule: a limit is jurisdictional only if Congress says so; Title VII's employee count is an element of the claim.
Removal in breach of the forum-defendant rule is a waivable defect: the plaintiff must object within 30 days, and the court cannot remand on its own.
Nonjurisdictional is not the same as flexible: the 30-day removal deadline cannot be equitably tolled.
Local actions: a trespass to land must be sued where the land lies, even if the defendant can be found elsewhere.
A state court rejects the local-action rule so that a wrongdoer cannot escape every court for harm to land in another state.
After the 1990 amendment venue lies wherever a substantial part of the events occurred, as where a collection notice was received.
Congress restates § 1391 and provides that venue is set without regard to whether an action is local or transitory.
Section 1404(a) lets a federal court transfer a case for convenience instead of dismissing it for forum non conveniens.
Transfer only to a district where the plaintiff could have sued when the case began; the defendant's consent cannot add one.
Forum non conveniens: a foreign plaintiff's choice gets less deference, and less favorable foreign law is ordinarily not decisive.
A multidistrict pretrial court must return each case for trial; it cannot use § 1404(a) to keep cases for itself.

key: Venue Clarification Act allows transfer by consent
note: The 2011 venue act lets courts transfer to any district all parties consent to, undoing Hoffman's limit.
A valid forum clause is enforced by § 1404(a) transfer, or by forum non conveniens for a non-federal forum, not by dismissal for improper venue.
A freely negotiated forum clause is prima facie valid in admiralty, enforced unless unreasonable or unjust, or tainted by fraud or overreaching.
In a diversity case § 1404(a), not state law, governs a clause's effect on transfer; the clause is a significant factor in the balance.
A clause in a non-negotiated form ticket is enforceable if reasonable and fundamentally fair; lack of bargaining does not void it.
A valid clause controls transfer in all but unusual cases: the plaintiff's choice and private interests get no weight.
Absent members are bound by a class judgment only if the parties to the suit adequately represented their interests.

The 1966 rewrite replaces the true/hybrid/spurious categories with Rule 23(a) and (b), including notice and exclusion rights for (b)(3) damages classes. It reforms procedure rather than merely codifying Hansberry.
Individual notice to every reasonably identifiable (b)(3) member, at the plaintiff's cost, with no merits preview to shift that cost.
A class judgment precludes only what it decided: losing a pattern-or-practice claim does not bar members' individual claims.
Absent plaintiffs can be bound without minimum contacts if they get notice, a chance to opt out and adequate representation.
A settlement class must still satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b); a fair deal cannot replace predominance and adequate representation.
A mandatory limited-fund class needs a fund shown to be truly limited, all of it devoted to the claims, and equitable treatment.

The FAA preempts California’s rule conditioning arbitration on class procedures. That removes this state-law obstacle to the agreement; it is not a holding that every class waiver is valid under every applicable defense.
Commonality needs a common question whose answer drives the case; individual backpay claims cannot proceed in a (b)(2) class.
The Ninth Circuit rejects a separate administrative-feasibility test: Rule 23's listed requirements already deal with identifying members.

The Seventh Circuit holds that a federal Rule 23 action under a federal statute needs personal jurisdiction for the named plaintiff, without a separate showing for each absentee. This is a circuit holding, not a Supreme Court resolution of every class setting.
Every class member who seeks damages must have standing; a statutory violation without concrete harm is not enough.
Summary judgment is improper if there is the slightest doubt about the facts, especially when a witness's credibility is at stake.
The hope that a jury will disbelieve the other side's witnesses is not evidence; a party with the burden needs proof of its own.
Summary judgment should be used sparingly in complex antitrust cases where motive and intent matter and the proof lies with the other side.
When the facts turn on the motive and credibility of the movant's own witnesses, the opponent may test them by cross-examination at trial.
The movant must foreclose any genuine issue; if its own showing leaves a gap, the motion fails even without a response.
Evidence as consistent with lawful competition as with conspiracy cannot carry an implausible conspiracy claim to a jury.
A dispute is genuine only if a reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant under the burden of proof that applies at trial.

After adequate time for discovery, a movant without the trial burden may identify the absence of evidence on an essential element without negating it. Only after that initial showing must the opponent identify a genuine jury issue.
A court need not accept a version of events that the record, such as a video, so blatantly contradicts that no jury could believe it.
Courts must still credit the nonmovant's evidence and may not resolve genuine disputes for the movant, even in qualified-immunity cases.
Under the code, claims arising from one transaction may be joined though they fall in different categories, such as false imprisonment and slander.
'Transaction' is a flexible word: a counterclaim arises from it when logically related to the claim, though the facts differ.
Rule 14 allows adjudication of contingent derivative indemnity before the defendant pays the plaintiff. It accelerates procedure without creating the substantive indemnity right.
Crossclaims and claims against added parties arise from the same transaction when logically related, with separate trials to manage them.
A counterclaim logically related to the claim is compulsory under Rule 13(a), and it comes within ancillary jurisdiction.
Plaintiffs may join when their claims arise from a series of logically related events and share a common question, as with a company-wide policy.
An absentee is indispensable only if any decree would inevitably affect its interest; separable interests let the court proceed.
The rewritten Rule 19 drops fixed labels for a two-step test: who should be joined, then whether to go on without them.
Indispensability is the conclusion of a practical weighing of everyone's interests in equity and good conscience, not a label applied first.
Joint tortfeasors are permissive parties, not required ones, so Rule 19(b) is never reached for them.
Where an immune sovereign with a nonfrivolous claim cannot be joined and could be harmed, the action must ordinarily be dismissed.

Statutory interpleader requires adverse claimants with minimal diversity, a stake worth at least $500, and deposit of the stake or a qualifying bond. The 1936 Act broadens access; these conditions still matter.
A disinterested tenant may interplead its landlord and a rival claimant despite the rule that a tenant may not deny the landlord's title.
An insurer may interplead tort claimants whose claims may exceed its policy limit, though it denies liability and the claims are unliquidated.
Minimal diversity suffices and interpleader may come before judgment, but it protects only the fund and cannot force all claims into one court.

Congress creates the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation and lets it send civil actions in different districts that share common questions of fact to one district for coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings, each to be remanded for trial unless already ended. The statute codified the practice used for the 1,800 electrical-equipment antitrust cases of the early 1960s.

A transferee court deciding a federal question applies its own circuit's law, considering but not bound by the transferor circuit; Van Dusen's rule that transferor law travels with the case is for state law in diversity (D.C. Circuit, Ginsburg, J.).

After the Panel gathered the federal asbestos cases in one district, the parties built a nationwide settlement class there. The Court rejected it: centralization does not relax Rule 23, so a settlement class must still show predominance and adequate representation.

The transferee court cannot use § 1404(a) to assign a transferred case to itself for trial; § 1407 obliges the Panel to remand it when pretrial proceedings end, ending a thirty-year practice of self-assignment that the Panel's rules had allowed.

The Court restates the design: § 1407 centralizes pretrial work to eliminate duplicate discovery, avoid conflicting rulings and save the parties' and courts' time, and each action must be remanded at or before the end of pretrial proceedings unless it has already ended.

key: Panel centralizes the Volkswagen diesel cases
note: Marketing, sales-practice and product cases about Volkswagen diesel vehicles go to the Northern District of California for coordinated pretrial proceedings. The court's first order consolidates them for pretrial only, sweeps in later tag-along actions, and makes no one a party to an action it was not named in.
Because § 1407 transfer is a rule of venue, a party may waive Lexecon's remand right, but only by a waiver that is clear and unambiguous (Fifth Circuit).

Rule 42(a) consolidation does not merge distinct actions for finality. A final judgment in one constituent action can be immediately appealed while the others remain pending; Rule 42 consolidation and § 1407 transfer remain distinct mechanisms.

key: Panel refuses to centralize the Kaiser vaccine-exemption suits
note: Sixteen suits by workers whose religious-exemption requests Kaiser denied shared its policy, but each turned on the plaintiff's sincerity, duties and timing, so centralization would bring few efficiencies; courts can treat rulings in related cases as persuasive instead.

The first Federal Rule written for multidistrict litigation: after the Panel transfers actions, the transferee court should hold an initial management conference, take the parties' report on leadership counsel and other matters, and enter an initial management order that controls the proceedings.
Congress may make a law's revival turn on a fact the President finds and proclaims; that is not a transfer of lawmaking.
When Congress names the contingency and its consequence, the President who finds the fact acts as its agent, not as a lawmaker.
Congress may let an administrator fill in details by rule and make breaking those rules a crime that Congress itself defines and punishes.
The test is named: a delegation is valid if Congress lays down an intelligible principle to which the delegate must conform.
First invalidation: Congress let the President ban hot-oil shipments without stating a policy, a standard or the findings required.
Power to write binding codes for whole industries, guided only by general recovery aims, is an unconstitutional transfer of lawmaking.
Wartime price control stands: standards need only be definite enough for a court to tell whether Congress's will was obeyed.
A three-judge court upholds the wage-price freeze: text, purpose, history and implied limits can supply the standard; breadth alone is no defect.
A plurality reads the OSH Act narrowly to avoid a sweeping delegation; Justice Rehnquist alone would hold the delegation unconstitutional.
The Sentencing Commission passes the intelligible-principle test; only Scalia objects to lawmaking by a body with no other power to exercise.
An agency cannot cure a standardless delegation by limiting itself; 'requisite to protect the public health' is a sufficient principle.

Four Justices uphold the delegation after narrowing SORNA by interpretation. Alito supplies the fifth vote under existing doctrine while inviting reconsideration; three dissenters propose a stricter approach. No majority replaces the intelligible-principle test.
The Senate may not share in removing an executive officer; a statute making removal depend on its consent is invalid.
Congress may not appoint officers who enforce the law; officials it names may only gather information and investigate, as a committee could.
A one-House veto is lawmaking: once it delegates, Congress may alter the delegate's power only by bicameral passage and presentment.
Congress may not keep removal power, short of impeachment, over an officer who executes the law, because removal brings control.
The D.C. Circuit holds that Congress's own agents may not sit on an enforcement agency, even as nonvoting members.
When Congress vests an inferior officer's appointment in a department head, it may also restrict that officer's removal.
The President's power to remove officers he appoints with Senate consent is his alone; Congress may not make it depend on the Senate.
Congress may protect members of a quasi-legislative, quasi-judicial commission such as the FTC from removal except for cause.
The President may not remove a member of an adjudicatory body like the War Claims Commission merely to put his own appointee in its place, even when the statute says nothing about removal.
Congress may not keep for itself the power to remove an officer who executes the law; impeachment is its only removal tool.
The test turns functional: a good-cause limit on an inferior officer is valid unless it impedes the President's constitutional duties.
Two layers of for-cause protection between the President and officers who exercise executive power violate Article II.
A lone agency head wielding significant executive power may not be shielded; exceptions stay with multimember bodies and some inferior officers.

Seila’s single-director rule reaches the FHFA. Because the officer was properly appointed, the unconstitutional removal restriction does not automatically invalidate past actions; retrospective relief requires compensable harm caused by the restriction.
Humphrey's Executor overruled: FTC commissioners exercise executive power and must be removable at will; the Federal Reserve is reserved.

The Court denies a stay of Cook’s preliminary protection: removal is reviewable and the statute requires notice and an opportunity to respond. It treats the Federal Reserve’s history separately and leaves the precise definition of cause open.
Congress may add duties germane to an existing office without requiring a fresh appointment of the officer who holds it.
Anyone exercising significant authority under federal law is an officer, appointed only as Article II allows; Congress may not appoint.
An independent counsel, removable for cause and limited in duties, jurisdiction and tenure, is an inferior officer whom a court may appoint.
Tax Court special trial judges are officers, not employees, and the Tax Court is a 'Court of Law' that may appoint them.
Assuming Shoemaker's germaneness principle applies, commissioned officers need no second appointment to serve as military judges, a duty germane to their office.
Inferior officers are those directed and supervised by Senate-confirmed officers; significant authority marks an officer, not a principal one.
The recess route is bounded: the Senate is in session when it says it is, and a break of under ten days is presumptively too short.
SEC administrative law judges are officers under Freytag, so appointment by staff was invalid; the cure is a new hearing before another official.
An inferior officer may not issue final decisions that no principal officer can review; the PTO Director must be able to review the Board.
Political discretion belongs to the executive, but a specific legal duty on which a person's rights depend can be enforced in court.
Where Congress has said how a law is to be executed, executive instructions cannot authorize more or shield the officer who obeys them.
The duty to execute the laws implies no power to dispense with them; a court may compel an officer's ministerial duty by mandamus.
Executive duties may be implied from the Constitution and general statutes, such as protecting a federal judge, not only from express laws.

Without a statute specifically authorizing the suit, but resting on Congress's commerce and postal legislation, the national government may sue in equity to stop forcible obstruction of interstate commerce and the mails.
Long executive practice known to Congress and left undisturbed implies its consent, here to the President's withdrawal of public lands.
The steel seizure fails: power must come from statute or the Constitution; Jackson's concurrence sorts action by Congress's will.
Jackson's categories become a spectrum: congressional acquiescence supports suspending claims, though the President has no plenary settlement power.
At the stay stage, the Guard statute likely requires lawful authority to use the regular military, which an asserted protective power did not supply.
When Congress leaves an agency to apply a term like 'producer' to particular facts, a reasoned application after a fair hearing stands.
The Board's application of 'employee' is accepted if it has warrant in the record and a reasonable basis in law.
Agency interpretations do not bind courts but carry weight from their care, reasoning, consistency and power to persuade.
Two steps: if Congress spoke to the precise question, that controls; if the statute is silent or ambiguous, a permissible agency reading wins.
Step zero: Chevron applies only where Congress gave power to act with the force of law and the agency used it; otherwise Skidmore.
A court's earlier reading yields to a later reasonable agency reading unless the court held that the statute was unambiguous.
Chevron applies even when the ambiguity concerns the scope of the agency's own authority.
A question of deep economic and political significance is not implicitly left to the agency; the Court reads the statute itself.
Auer (Seminole Rock) deference to an agency's reading of its own rule survives, but only for genuine ambiguity and an authoritative, expert reading.
Chevron overruled: under APA § 706 courts decide what statutes mean independently, honoring real delegations and giving agency views Skidmore weight.
Absent a clear mandate, the plurality will not read the OSH Act to give the agency unprecedented power over American industry.
In extraordinary cases courts hesitate to find an implicit delegation over a large part of the economy; Congress had not given the FDA power to regulate tobacco products as customarily marketed.
A question of deep economic and political significance was not left to the IRS; the Court decides it by reading the whole statute.
A nationwide eviction moratorium needs clear authorization; a general disease-control power read with its narrow examples does not give it.
A vaccine-or-test mandate for large employers is a general public-health measure, not an occupational standard Congress clearly authorized.
The same day, a vaccination rule for health-care staff stands: it falls within express power to protect patients' health and safety.
The doctrine is named: in extraordinary cases the agency must point to clear congressional authorization; a merely plausible reading is not enough.
Power to 'waive or modify' allows modest changes, not mass loan cancellation; Barrett recasts the doctrine as reading text in context.
Government employment is a privilege, not property, so dismissal needs no due process; an equally divided Court affirmed in 1951.
Officials may not cost a person a private job through a clearance hearing without confrontation unless Congress or the President expressly allows it.
No hearing was due to bar a cook from a naval base: the process due depends on the government function and the private interest at stake.
Welfare benefits are a statutory entitlement, not a privilege, so ending them triggers due process and a prior hearing.
Property means a legitimate claim of entitlement from an independent source such as state law; a one-year appointment gives none.
Mutually explicit understandings, not only formal tenure, can create a property interest in continued public employment.
A three-Justice plurality says a statute granting a job may also limit its procedures, the 'bitter with the sweet'; six Justices disagree.
State law creates the interest, but the Constitution sets the procedure for taking it away; the bitter-with-the-sweet idea is rejected.
Meeting eligibility criteria is no entitlement when supply is limited and officials have unrestricted discretion over who gets the benefit.
A Colorado court holds that a no-entitlement clause does not defeat a property interest where officials cannot deny funded benefits to the eligible.
When a body assesses particular owners on individual grounds, each must get notice and a hearing with argument and proof.
A general rule applied to everyone alike needs no individual hearing; the check on it is political, not procedural.
Welfare may not be cut off before an evidentiary hearing with oral presentation, confrontation and an impartial decisionmaker.
Three-factor balancing of private interest, risk of error and government burden; no evidentiary hearing is needed before disability benefits stop.
School paddling implicates liberty, but common-law limits and later civil and criminal remedies supply the process due; no prior hearing.
A customer facing a utility shutoff must be told how to dispute the bill and get a chance to present it to someone able to fix it.
Before firing a tenured employee: notice, an explanation of the evidence and a chance to respond, with a fuller hearing afterward.
Before an order reinstating a whistleblower, the employer gets the substance of the evidence and a chance to respond, not a trial-type hearing.
Mathews, modified to weigh the plaintiff's interest, governs private prejudgment attachment; attaching a home without notice or exigency fails.
After a lawful seizure the owner must be told of it, but not of return remedies set out in published statutes and cases.
Where an ordinary contract suit can fully protect a disputed claim for payment, that suit is all the process due.
Matters of public right, like summary collection of a revenue officer's debt, may be settled by the executive without an Article III trial.
When the Government enforces new statutory public rights, Congress may assign penalty cases to an agency forum with no jury.
A government suit for civil penalties is legal in nature, so the defendant gets a jury on liability, though the judge sets the amount.
Calling a claim a core proceeding cannot strip the jury right; a traditional legal claim against a stranger to the estate is no public right.

SEC fraud penalties resemble a common-law legal claim and require an Article III jury. The Court distinguishes Atlas Roofing rather than overruling it; public rights and other kinds of agency adjudication remain separate questions.
A court judges an agency order only on the grounds the agency invoked; it may not supply a policy judgment the agency never made.
The concise statement of basis and purpose need not answer every comment but must show the major issues and why the agency chose as it did.
Courts ask whether the agency took a 'hard look' and engaged in reasoned decisionmaking; if it did, they defer even if they would differ.
Review is searching and careful, on the full administrative record: did the agency weigh the relevant factors, or make a clear error of judgment?
A discretionary requirement fails when the agency does not tie it to the statute's goal or answer concrete objections in the record.
An agency may base standards on predicted technology if it answers objections and gives plausible reasons each remaining step can be done in time.
The core test: examine the data and connect facts to choice; rescinding a rule gets the same review, and counsel's later reasons do not count.
After State Farm's remand, the new passive-restraint rule's present choices survive as reasonably explained; its contingent parts are unripe.
A policy change needs no better reasons than the old policy: acknowledge the change, give good reasons, and address reliance and prior findings.
The stated reason must be the real one: when the explanation does not match the record, the action goes back to the agency.
Rescinding a program requires weighing reliance and alternatives within it; reasons offered later cannot save the original action.

A legal error in an agency’s discretionary reasoning ordinarily requires Chenery remand; the court may not simply substitute its own corrected analysis. Narrow remand exceptions are not a general license to supply agency policy.
Failing to respond to a significant comment likely makes a rule arbitrary and capricious, and that defect can support a stay.
Substantial evidence is judged on the whole record, including evidence that detracts from the finding and the examiner's contrary report.
Examining physicians' written reports can be substantial evidence despite hearsay and contrary testimony when the claimant could have subpoenaed them.
Substantial-evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious review demand the same factual support; the former simply confines it to a formal record.
A health standard may rest on cumulative, imperfect science, but the agency must show with evidence why a feasible added protection is unneeded.
An agency must apply the standard it announces; a finding that quietly demands more than that standard lacks substantial evidence.
The APA's standards govern review of the patent office's fact findings; the stricter clear-error test courts apply to judges does not.
Informal action needs the same evidentiary support as formal action, drawn from what the agency had before it when it acted.
The threshold is not high and is applied case by case; an expert's refusal to share underlying data does not automatically defeat it.
'Committed to agency discretion' is a narrow exception for cases with no law to apply; statutory standards make action reviewable.
A decision not to sue to set aside a union election is reviewable, but only for rationality, on the Secretary's statement of reasons.
A refusal to enforce is presumptively unreviewable unless the statute supplies guidelines that limit the agency's enforcement discretion.
A refusal to begin rulemaking is reviewable under a highly deferential standard but still needs a reasoned, record-supported explanation.
A court may compel only a discrete action the agency is legally required to take, not general compliance with a broad mandate.
Denying a rulemaking petition is reviewable, and the agency's reasons must track the statute's criteria, not unrelated policy preferences.
Ending a program that solicits applications and grants benefits is more than passive nonenforcement, so Heckler's presumption does not bar review.
The APA sorts agency action into two kinds, each with its own procedure: rules, which have future effect, and orders, the products of adjudication.
The choice between a general rule and case-by-case adjudication is primarily the agency's; retroactive effect is weighed, not fatal.
No majority: a plurality says a purely prospective rule announced in adjudication evades the APA, but the order against the party is enforced.

The D.C. Circuit reads the FTC Act’s general rulemaking clause to authorize binding rules defining unfair or deceptive practices. The holding concerns that statutory scheme, not every agency’s general rulemaking clause.
The Board may announce new principles through adjudication; the choice is reviewed only for abuse, as where it would upset reliance.
The APA requires notice, written comment and a statement of basis and purpose; trial-type procedure only when rules must be made on the record.
In on-the-record rulemaking, parties must be able to test the data behind the agency's summaries, or the findings lack support.
Formal rulemaking applies only when a statute calls for rules 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing' or the like.
Even short of formal procedure, a rule under substantial-evidence review needs a record whose factual premises parties could test.

A separate adjudication branch: the Ninth Circuit reads a statutory “public hearing” on disputed facts to trigger formal APA adjudication without “on the record.” This does not expand formal rulemaking under Florida East Coast.
Notice must disclose the scientific data behind a proposal, and the final statement must answer comments that go to the rule's core.
Courts may not add procedures to informal rulemaking beyond those the Constitution, the APA and the governing statute require.
The disclosure rule survives Vermont Yankee: studies the agency relies on must be released for comment; Judge Kavanaugh questions it.
Vermont Yankee applied: interpretive rules need no notice and comment, even when they change an earlier interpretation.
Courts may not add an open-mindedness test to notice and comment; the APA's objective requirements, if met, are enough.
A final rule must be a logical outgrowth of the proposal; the Fifth Circuit held the pistol-brace rule was not, so its challengers were likely to succeed.
A policy statement only announces what the agency intends; not being a binding norm, it is exempt, but must be defended each time it is applied.
A pronouncement with present binding effect that leaves the agency no real discretion is a legislative rule, whatever its label.

The D.C. Circuit lists indicia of legislative rules: an independent enforcement basis, CFR publication, express legislative authority or amendment of a legislative rule. Later cases focus on legal effect; publication alone is not a universal conclusive test.
A requirement that cannot be derived from a regulation by interpretation, such as a flat eight-foot fence height, is legislative.
Guidance explaining a duty within a regulation is interpretive, but a definitive interpretation may not be fundamentally revised without comment.
Guidance that states a settled position and binds in practice is reviewable final action and cannot expand a rule without rulemaking.
A document labeled guidance is a legislative rule when its text binds both the regulated parties and the agency itself.
The Paralyzed Veterans revision rule is abrogated: interpretive rules are exempt from notice and comment whether new or changed.
A deferred-action program that in practice leaves officials no real discretion is likely a substantive rule needing notice and comment.
A rule is interpretive only if the statute or rule it explains compels or logically justifies it; guidance that makes new law is legislative.
The threshold becomes injury in fact, economic or otherwise, replacing the older demand for an established legal interest.
Aesthetic and environmental harm counts as injury, but the plaintiff or its members must suffer it; concern for a cause is not enough.
Injury must be concrete, particularized and imminent, traceable and redressable; a citizen-suit provision cannot dispense with it.
Legislators lack standing for an abstract dilution of institutional power, and a statute authorizing their suit cannot supply the injury.
Denial of information a statute requires to be disclosed is a concrete injury, even though many voters share it.
Reasonable concerns that curtail use of a river are injury, and civil penalties paid to the Treasury redress it by deterrence.
States get special solicitude: a threatened coastline and a procedural right let Massachusetts challenge EPA's refusal to regulate.
Injury must be concrete as well as particularized; a bare procedural violation of a statute is not automatically enough.
A provision with no penalty and no enforcement causes no traceable injury, so the individual and state challengers lacked standing.

Every member recovering damages needs concrete injury. For intangible injury the Court asks for a close historical analogue; an unmaterialized risk alone does not support retrospective damages, though prospective relief is a separate inquiry.
States' indirect costs give them no judicially cognizable interest in forcing the Executive to make more arrests.
Responsible representatives of the listening public, not only economic competitors, may intervene to contest a broadcast license renewal.
Beyond injury, the plaintiff's interest need only be arguably within the zone of interests the statute protects or regulates.
The zone test is not demanding: it bars only interests so marginal to the statute that Congress cannot be assumed to have meant them to sue.
The zone is set by the statute whose violation is claimed; postal workers' job interests fall outside the postal monopoly laws.
An agency's policy interest does not make it 'adversely affected or aggrieved'; the Director could not appeal a worker's award.
The zone is drawn from the particular provision invoked, and economic interests in avoiding needless regulation can fall within it.
A plaintiff need not show that Congress meant to benefit it; banks are arguably within the zone of a credit-union membership limit.
Title VII's 'person aggrieved' means the zone of interests, which covers an employee fired to punish a co-worker's charge.
The test is lenient: a neighbor's economic, environmental and aesthetic interests are arguably within a land-acquisition statute.
Interests that align with a statute's beneficiaries only by accident, as paper sellers' do under securities law, fall outside the zone.
An organization may sue for members who are themselves injured; its long-standing interest in a cause does not give it standing.
An organization has standing in its own right when the defendant's practices perceptibly impair its services and drain its resources.
Hunt's three-part test for associational standing is reaffirmed, and a class action is not a required substitute for it.
Conflicts among members do not defeat associational standing, but the members represented must themselves have standing.
Hunt's third prong is prudential, not constitutional, so Congress may let a union sue for its members' damages.
A genuine voluntary membership organization that meets Hunt has standing; its members need not also control or fund it.
General words of a statute yield to its purpose and to the maxim that no one may profit from his own wrong: the murderer does not inherit.
A case within the letter may fall outside the statute when its history, context and consequences show the legislature did not mean it.
Legislative history may be consulted even when the words of a statute seem clear on first reading.
When a literal reading gives odd results and raises constitutional doubts, purpose and history support a narrower reading of 'utilized'.
Textualism gains ground: 'attorney's fee' does not include expert fees, and courts may not supplement clear text with purpose.
The Second Circuit finds 'any court' ambiguous in context and, relying on legislative history, reads it to exclude foreign convictions.
The Court reaches the same result by presuming that Congress legislates with domestic concerns in mind; three Justices dissent on the text.
Text controls over a conference report: a fee condition on federal funds needs clear notice, and legislative history cannot supply it.
Ordinary meaning and mechanics decide: a bump stock does not fire more than one shot by a single function of the trigger.
Ordinary meaning cuts both ways: some parts kits and unfinished frames are covered, so the agency's rule is not facially invalid.
'Vehicle' after a list of land vehicles means things that move on land, and a criminal law must give fair warning; airplanes are out.
Ejusdem generis: 'other dangerous weapon' after dagger, dirk and stiletto reaches stabbing weapons, not a rifle.
Noscitur a sociis and consistent usage: 'communication' in the prospectus definition means public solicitations, not a private sale contract.
The Second Circuit reads 'negligent transmission' with 'loss' and 'miscarriage': it covers harm to the mail, not injury from a misplaced package.
The Court resolves the circuit split the same way: the postal exception covers mail lost, late, damaged or misdelivered, not every delivery mishap.
Ejusdem generis limits the NLRA's 'other concerted activities' to things like organizing and bargaining, not class procedures.

Under UCC §2-313, a seller's affirmation of fact or description creates an express warranty without formal words or intent to warrant, and it is presumed to be part of the basis of the bargain unless the seller proves otherwise.

A seller's statement creates an express warranty only if it is an affirmation, promise or description relating to the goods actually sold that forms part of the basis of the bargain; statements about differently configured goods and general commendation do not.

Under the implied warranty of merchantability, fitness for ordinary purposes is measured by the reasonable expectations of an ordinary user or purchaser, not by the subjective expectations of the particular person who used the product.

Under New York UCC §2-316(2) and §1-201(b)(10), a written disclaimer of implied warranties is conspicuous if a reasonable person ought to notice it from its overall presentation, and the statute sets no absolute rule that it must appear before the signature.
A moral obligation or gratitude for a benefit already conferred, without a prior request or an existing legal obligation of the promisor, is not consideration for a later express promise to pay.

A moral obligation coupled with a material benefit actually received by the promisor, such as having his life saved, can support his later express promise to pay, even without a prior bargain or an original duty to pay.

A worker who leaves an entire labor contract without good cause cannot recover on the contract but may recover in quantum meruit the reasonable value of the benefit the employer retained, less the damage caused by the breach and capped by the contract price.
